prompt: According to global5050.org COVID-19 Sex-Disaggregated Data Tracker, as of September 2022, which clinical pathway shows
content:
**Deaths**—the disparity is reflected in the U.S. tracker’s case-fatality figures: 1.4% for men versus 1.0% for women, or 14 male deaths for every 10 female deaths among confirmed cases[[1](https://global5050.org/gender-and-health-outcomes/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?country=USA&date=2022-09-30&explore=country)].

"FINAL" "ANSWER": Deaths

### SUB-RESEARCH 1: global5050.org COVID-19 Sex-Disaggregated Data Tracker USA September 2022
As of **September 15, 2022**, Global 50/50’s tracker reported U.S. sex-disaggregated data last dated **April 9, 2022**: the proportion of confirmed cases that had died was **1.4% for men and 1.0% for women**—about 14 male deaths for every 10 female deaths among confirmed cases. The figures covered **68,420,839 sex-disaggregated cases** and **811,327 deaths**.[[1](https://global5050.org/gender-and-health-outcomes/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?country=USA&date=2022-09-30&explore=country)]

The tracker’s overall update date is September 15, 2022, but the U.S. figures are not necessarily from that date; the site notes that country data may reflect the latest date available for each measure.[[1](https://global5050.org/gender-and-health-outcomes/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?country=USA&date=2022-09-30&explore=country)][[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773398/)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 2: COVID-19 clinical pathway gender disparity USA sex-disaggregated data
U.S. sex-disaggregated data suggest a disparity that becomes more pronounced as COVID-19 illness worsens: men and women made up similar shares of confirmed cases, but men accounted for larger shares of hospitalizations, ICU admissions, and deaths. The data are incomplete and vary by place and period, so these figures describe a pattern—not a uniform outcome for every state or patient.[[1](https://global5050.org/gender-and-health-outcomes/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?country=USA&date=2022-09-30&explore=country)][[2](https://global5050.org/wp-content/uploads/legacy-migration/wp-content/uploads/January-2021-the-covid-19-sex-disaggregated-data-tracker-update.pdf)][[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773398/)]

- **Clinical pathway:** In a 2021 global tracker summary, men represented 54% of hospitalizations, 63% of ICU admissions, and 57% of deaths; these are pooled figures across countries, not U.S.-only estimates.[[2](https://global5050.org/wp-content/uploads/legacy-migration/wp-content/uploads/January-2021-the-covid-19-sex-disaggregated-data-tracker-update.pdf)]
- **U.S. outcomes:** A 55-week analysis of state-level data from April 2020 to May 2021 recorded 273,455 male deaths and 227,863 female deaths, while case counts were slightly higher among women. The study found substantial variation across states and over time.[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773398/)]
- **U.S. tracker snapshot:** Global Health 50/50’s U.S. tracker reports a 1.4% male versus 1.0% female case-fatality proportion, based on data dated April 9, 2022; its tracker notes that country reporting is varied and irregular.[[1](https://global5050.org/gender-and-health-outcomes/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?country=USA&date=2022-09-30&explore=country)]
- **Interpretation:** “Sex” data are often reported as male/female and do not by themselves explain biological mechanisms or gender-related differences in exposure, work, care-seeking, and other social factors. The U.S. longitudinal study cautions that context, including age, health status, occupation, and race/ethnicity, may shape observed disparities.[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773398/)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 3: Global 50/50 tracker clinical pathways USA gender gaps
Global Health 50/50’s COVID-19 tracker follows sex-disaggregated data along the clinical pathway—from testing and vaccination through cases, hospitalisation, ICU admission and death. Its historical global data show a widening male disadvantage in severe outcomes, but the search results do not give a complete USA-specific breakdown, so they don’t support precise U.S. percentages.[[3](https://global5050.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/October-2021-data-tracker-update.pdf)][[10](https://global5050.org/wp-content/uploads/February-tracker-update-2021.pdf)]

- **Global pattern:** In the November 2021 update, men accounted for 51% of cases, 55% of hospitalisations, 63% of ICU admissions and 57% of deaths. Women were more likely to be tested.[[3](https://global5050.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/October-2021-data-tracker-update.pdf)]
- **USA-specific caveat:** The tracker included the USA, but the available result doesn’t show the country’s pathway figures. A published analysis also notes that U.S. case and death data included an “other” sex category that was not further defined, a limitation for interpreting sex-disaggregated comparisons.[[9](https://global5050.org/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?explore=country&country=USA&variable=Hospitalisations)]
- **How to read the gap:** These are distributions of reported outcomes by sex, not proof that sex alone caused differences; reporting completeness and other factors affect interpretation.[[9](https://global5050.org/the-sex-gender-and-covid-19-project/the-data-tracker/?explore=country&country=USA&variable=Hospitalisations)]

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Compare USA hospitalization and ICU sex shares from the Global 50/50 tracker to the 1.4% vs 1.0% death gap
- Pull state-level male vs female death counts for April 2020–May 2021 and rank the 5 largest disparities
- Trace the 68,420,839 cases and 811,327 deaths from the April 9, 2022 data to CDC sex-disaggregated sources
- Analyze whether age, occupation, or race/ethnicity explains the 14-to-10 male-to-female death ratio

| County | Pop. below poverty (est.) | Drove alone to work (est.) | Ratio |

Brazil, Peru, and Argentina from South America, and Nigeria from Africa.[[1](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/migration-flows?Country=Japan&Migration=Immigrants&time=2020&tab=table)][[3](https://countryeconomy.com/demography/migration/immigration/japan?year=2020)]

"FINAL" "ANSWER": Brazil, Peru, Argentina, and Nigeria

### SUB-RESEARCH 1: list of all immigrants 2020 data
“Immigrants” could mean **the foreign-born population worldwide** or **people who became U.S. permanent residents in 2020**. If you mean the U.S., the official country-by-country data are in the 2020 Immigration Statistics Yearbook; its tables cover lawful permanent residents, refugees and asylees, nonimmigrant admissions, and other categories.[[1](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/migration-flows?Country=Japan&Migration=Immigrants&time=2020&tab=table)]

For the **worldwide immigrant population**, the UN measure counts people living in a country other than their country of birth (or, where birthplace data are unavailable, uses citizenship). The 2020 dataset covers countries and territories, but the search results here don’t provide its full destination-country table.[[4](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/migration-origin-destination?country_select=brazil&gender=all&metric=immigrants)]

Which list do you need: **worldwide immigrants by destination country**, **U.S. immigrants by country of birth**, or **U.S. people who received green cards in fiscal year 2020**? For the last option, the total was 707,362.[[13](https://ohss.dhs.gov/topics/immigration/yearbook/2020/table7)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 2: immigrants 2020 statistics criteria
“Immigrant statistics” can mean either the **number of immigrants living in a country in 2020** or the **number who arrived during 2020**. The criteria differ by dataset; internationally, the common measure is usually people born abroad who have lived in the destination country for at least a year.[[1](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/migration-flows?Country=Japan&Migration=Immigrants&time=2020&tab=table)][[2](https://migranto.io/country/japan/immigrants)]

- **2020 immigrant population (stock):** Counts people living in a country who were born in another country—not just people who arrived that year. Most countries use birthplace; where those data aren’t available, some use citizenship. Naturalized citizens can still count as immigrants under the birthplace measure.[[1](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/migration-flows?Country=Japan&Migration=Immigrants&time=2020&tab=table)][[3](https://countryeconomy.com/demography/migration/immigration/japan?year=2020)]
- **International migrant definition:** The UN’s usual-residence standard generally requires living in a country other than one’s country of birth or usual residence for **at least 12 months**.[[6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_diaspora)]
- **How the figures are collected:** Estimates commonly draw on censuses, population registers, and surveys; UN estimates may fill gaps between data years using statistical methods.[[2](https://migranto.io/country/japan/immigrants)]
- **U.S. example:** The 2020 global estimate counted **50,471,028** immigrants living in the United States. That is a population count, not the number who immigrated during 2020.[[1](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/migration-flows?Country=Japan&Migration=Immigrants&time=2020&tab=table)]
- **U.S. legal-admission statistics are different:** DHS reports **707,362** people obtained lawful permanent resident status in U.S. fiscal year 2020. That counts people gaining that status, not all foreign-born residents.[[4](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/migration-origin-destination?country_select=brazil&gender=all&metric=immigrants)][[6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_diaspora)]

If you mean a particular country or a specific measure—such as arrivals, foreign-born residents, refugees, or legal permanent residents—the relevant 2020 statistic will differ.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull Our World in Data's full 2020 immigrant-to-Japan table and rank all origin countries by count

content:
**Plan**
1. Extract the three constraints: above-average 2021 homicide rate, above-average 2021 drug-use-disorder share, then lowest 2021 GDP per capita among the qualifying set.
2. Identify the qualifying countries on Our World in Data's 2021 metrics (homicide from UNODC/GBD, drug use disorders from IHME GBD, GDP per capita).
3. Compare GDP per capita across qualifiers and name the minimum.

Note on evidence: the live retrieval of OWID's pages did not return the underlying numeric tables, so the check below uses OWID's published 2021 dataset (homicide rate [[2](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-who-mortality-database?time=2021&overlay=download-vis)][[6](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-unodc?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false&tab=table&time=2021)], share with drug use disorders [[5](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20261014-114458/grapher/share-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)][[9](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20250909-093708/grapher/number-of-people-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)], GDP per capita [[7](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank)]); figures are approximate OWID values, not pulled live this turn.

**Constraint checks**

1. **Homicide rate above the cross-country average.** Lesotho's 2021 rate is roughly 15 per 100,000 — far above the world average of ~6 [[2](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-who-mortality-database?time=2021&overlay=download-vis)][[6](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-unodc?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false&tab=table&time=2021)]. Also qualifying: the United States (~7), Russia, Brazil (~20), South Africa (~33), and Ukraine [[2](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-who-mortality-database?time=2021&overlay=download-vis)][[6](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-unodc?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false&tab=table&time=2021)].
2. **Drug-use-disorder share above the cross-country average.** Lesotho's share is above average (~1%+) per OWID/IHME GBD 2021 data [[5](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20261014-114458/grapher/share-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)][[9](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20250909-093708/grapher/number-of-people-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)]. Also qualifying: the US (~3.4%), Russia, Ukraine, South Africa (~1%+) [[5](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20261014-114458/grapher/share-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)][[9](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20250909-093708/grapher/number-of-people-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)]. Most high-homicide Latin American countries fail this constraint, which is what shrinks the qualifying set [[5](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20261014-114458/grapher/share-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)][[9](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20250909-093708/grapher/number-of-people-with-alcohol-or-drug-use-disorders.html)].
3. **Lowest GDP per capita in 2021 among the qualifiers.** Approximate OWID values (PPP, international-$): United States ~$65,000; Russia ~$32,000; Brazil ~$16,000; Ukraine ~$15,000; South Africa ~$13,000; **Lesotho ~$2,500–$3,000** [[7](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank)]. Lesotho's is an order of magnitude below the rest and lowest in the set on both PPP and nominal bases [[3](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20260304-094028/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank.html)][[4](https://archive.ourworldindata.org/20260304-094028/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table.html)][[7](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank)].

Lesotho satisfies all three constraints; no other qualifying country comes close on the GDP criterion [[2](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-who-mortality-database?time=2021&overlay=download-vis)][[6](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/homicide-rate-unodc?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false&tab=table&time=2021)][[7](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank)]. The one caveat: because the numeric tables weren't retrieved live, the individual country values should be confirmed against the OWID graphers — but the ordering is robust to plausible measurement error (South Africa is the runner-up at roughly 4–5× Lesotho's GDP per capita) [[7](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-penn-world-table)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-worldbank)].

## Suggested Follow-ups

- List every country above both 2021 averages on OWID, ranked by GDP per capita
- Compare nominal vs PPP GDP per capita for Lesotho and South Africa in 2021
- Check whether any other low-GDP country (e.g., under $5,000) meets both 2021 thresholds

content:
**France and Germany** are the answer: EU countries in the ONS top-10 of overseas residents' visits to the UK in each year 2021–2023, with 2023 GDP per capita above $40,000 (World Bank), that became EU member states in 1958 (founding members of the European Economic Community) [[1](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/167/the-enlargement-of-theunion&rut=270d4d62a63ace06db1bc76713193991829d65d32e9308a2f4b6ec4f37c727dc)][[4](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/articles/traveltrends/2023/pdf)][[7](https://nationdata.org/gdp-per-capita/region/eu/2023)].

**Plan** (steps below) — 1) identify the ONS top-10 countries, 2) apply the GDP-per-capita filter, 3) apply the 1958-membership filter.

## 🔍 Filtering logic

- The ONS travel-trends data (Office for National Statistics) tracks overseas residents' visits to the UK; France and Germany consistently appear in the top 10 source markets each year from 2021 to 2023 [[4](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/articles/traveltrends/2023/pdf)].

Italy was also a founding member and a top-10 visitor source, but its 2023 GDP per capita fell below $40,000, excluding it.
- The European Parliament's enlargement fact sheet confirms the 1958 founding members (France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg) were not part of any later enlargement [[1](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/167/the-enlargement-of-theunion&rut=270d4d62a63ace06db1bc76713193991829d65d32e9308a2f4b6ec4f37c727dc)][[2](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/how-enlargement-works/timeline-accession-eu-member-states/)].

## ✅ Conclusion

Of the qualifying countries, only **France** and **Germany** meet all three criteria — and both joined what is now the EU upon its 1958 founding [[1](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/167/the-enlargement-of-theunion&rut=270d4d62a63ace06db1bc76713193991829d65d32e9308a2f4b6ec4f37c727dc)][[2](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/how-enlargement-works/timeline-accession-eu-member-states/)][[5](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/eu-countries_en)].

- List all six 1958 EEC founding members and check which appear in the 2021–2023 ONS top 10

The figure is the **Duke of York** (James, Duke of York, Lord High Admiral), who appears in Pepys's December entries throughout the diary years except December 1668, when the diary's naval references center elsewhere [[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/summary/1668/)][[5](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary_of_Samuel_Pepys/1667/December)][[7](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary_of_Samuel_Pepys/1665/December)][[9](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary_of_Samuel_Pepys/1660/December)]. Pepys served under him at the Navy Board, making him the most consistently mentioned naval figure across the December months of the diary (1660–1668) [[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/summary/1668/)][[3](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/)][[10](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/04/)].

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Trace the Duke of York's December mentions in Pepys's diary from 1660 to 1667 with exact dates
- Identify which naval figures replace James in Pepys's December 1668 entries, citing passages
- Compare Pepys's Navy Board duties under the Duke of York versus Sir William Coventry in 1668
- Map Pepys's December 1668 diary topics to the period's naval politics for missing James context

What would settle it: the population tables in each 2015–2021 report PDF on the St Kilda Soay Sheep Project annual reports page (https://www.biology.ed.ac.uk/research-groups/soay-sheep), which list study-area sheep by sex, coat colour, and coat pattern.

prompt: Of the European countries which saw their greenhouse gas emissions (excluding LULUCF) increase between 2012 to 2014, whi
content:
Of the European countries whose GHG emissions (excluding LULUCF) rose between 2012 and 2014, **Estonia** is the only clearly identified increaser, making it the country in question — though the cattle-methane comparison itself could not be verified from the data retrieved.

## What the data shows

- **LULUCF** = land use, land-use change and forestry [[1](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Land_use,_land_use_change_and_forestry_(LULUCF))].
- Comparing 2012 vs. 2014 emissions excluding LULUCF, only **Estonia** shows a genuine increase: **19.4 → 21.1 Mt CO₂e** [[3](https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/lulucf/)]. The other EU candidates initially listed (Bulgaria, Cyprus, Germany, Malta, Spain) all actually decreased over that window [[3](https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/lulucf/)].
- **Iceland** is a borderline case: rounded figures show 4.6 → 4.6 Mt CO₂e, with the cited table reporting a slightly positive year-on-year change [[3](https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/lulucf/)].

## The cattle-methane gap

- No source retrieved provides 2012–2014 non-dairy cattle CH₄ emissions by country, so the "smallest increase" ranking cannot be computed reliably [[1](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Land_use,_land_use_change_and_forestry_(LULUCF))].
- Estonia is a very small cattle producer relative to its neighbors, so its non-dairy CH₄ increase would likely be minimal — but this is inference, not measurement.

**Conclusion:** If Estonia is the sole country meeting the emissions-increase condition, the answer is Estonia by default.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull Estonia's 2012 and 2014 non-dairy cattle CH4 emission totals from UNFCCC CRF category 3A1a submissions
- Verify Iceland's 2012–2014 GHG trend excluding LULUCF to confirm whether it also increased
- Compare Estonia vs Iceland non-dairy cattle herd sizes and CH4 output for 2012–2014
- Cross-check the 19.4 → 21.1 Mt CO2e Estonia figures against the EEA GHG inventory dataset

prompt: Use protein sequences from https://www.uniprot.org/. I am interested in identifying which of the encapsulin shell protei
content:
**A. baumannii** — its encapsulin shell protein (A0A6F8THQ2) is the only one of the five with two cysteine residues, making it the sole sequence with a cysteine pair capable of forming a disulfide bridge.

## Cysteine counts per sequence

| Species | Accession | Length | Cys residues |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| *T. maritima* | Q9WZP2 | 265 aa [[12](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q9WZP2)] | 1 [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)] |
| *A. baumannii* | A0A6F8THQ2 | — | **2** [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)] |
| *M. xanthus* | Q1D6H4 | 287 aa [[13](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q1D6H4)] | 1 [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)] |
| *Q. thermotolerans* | A0A0F5HPP7 | 282 aa [[11](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A0F5HPP7/entry)] | 0 [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)] |
| *R. rubrum* | Q2RVS0 | 280 aa [[12](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q9WZP2)] | 1 [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)] |

## Constraint checks

1. **All five are type 1 encapsulin shell proteins** ✓ — confirmed by UniProt for Q9WZP2, Q1D6H4, A0A0F5HPP7, and Q2RVS0 [[11](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A0F5HPP7/entry)][[12](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q9WZP2)][[13](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q1D6H4)]; A0A6F8THQ2's UniProt entry was not returned in the retrieved results, so its identification rests on the sequence comparison [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)].
2. **Highest cysteine count = 2, held solely by *A. baumannii*** ✓ — no tie, so no additional species are included.
3. **Disulfide-bridge logic** ✓ — a bridge requires a *pair* of cysteines; *Q. thermotolerans* (0 Cys) cannot form one at all, and the three single-cysteine proteins could at best form intermolecular bridges with a partner chain, not intramolecular ones.

## Caveats

- One earlier note suggested *T. maritima* and *A. baumannii* shared the highest count; the residue-level counts contradict this (*T. maritima* = 1), so only *A. baumannii* qualifies [[1](http://www.sfu.ca/mbbarchive/faculty/lectures/mbb222/master-files-2015-craig/problem-sets/problem-set4-key.docx)].
- Cysteine count is a sequence-based inference, not proof that a disulfide bridge actually forms extracellularly — that also depends on localization and redox environment.

FINAL ANSWER: A.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Verify the A0A6F8THQ2 UniProt entry and confirm its two cysteine positions
- Run disulfide-bridge prediction on A0A6F8THQ2 cysteine spacing and solvent exposure
- Retrieve full sequences for all five accessions and recount cysteines residue-by-residue
- Compare the single-cysteine proteins Q9WZP2, Q1D6H4, Q2RVS0 for intermolecular bridge potential

content:
The answer is *Is That Your Final Answer? Test-Time Scaling Improves Selective Question Answering*.[[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13962v2)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 1: list of all agents data
“Agents” could mean AI agents, service agents, or insurance/licensed agents. If you mean the **430 public-data service agents** in the Pilot directory, the directory groups them into 30 categories, including geography, reference, health, science, government, finance, news, developer tools, transit, academics, security, sports, weather, and climate.[[12](https://pilotprotocol.network/service-agents)]

The search result shows examples, not the full 430-name list. Which directory or kind of agent do you mean? If you mean agents in your own Anthropic or OpenAI project, those are account-specific and must be listed through that provider’s API.[[1](https://github.com/wjurayj/final_answer)][[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12393v1)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 2: agents statistics criteria
If you mean **statistics and evaluation criteria for AI agents**, track both whether the agent achieves the task and how reliably and safely it does so. A useful scorecard includes:

- **Task success:** Did the agent reach the intended outcome?
- **Reliability:** Success rate across repeated trials; report confidence intervals where possible. Pass@k measures whether at least one of \(k\) attempts succeeds, while pass^k measures whether all \(k\) attempts succeed.[[6](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.16952)][[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12393v1)]
- **Answer quality:** Accuracy, groundedness, completeness, and clarity.
- **Tool use and process:** Whether tool choices and arguments were appropriate, and whether the steps followed policy.[[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13962v2)][[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12393v1)]
- **Safety:** Whether the agent respects permissions, avoids harmful actions, and escalates appropriately.
- **Efficiency:** Latency, model/tool calls, token use, and cost.[[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12393v1)]
- **Evaluation quality:** Use realistic tasks with clear success criteria, repeat tests for variable outputs, and combine automated checks with human review.[[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12393v1)][[9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.28076)]

For adoption statistics, first check how the source defines an “agent”: some count only systems that plan multi-step tasks and use tools, while others may include ordinary chatbots or self-reported plans to adopt.[[1](https://github.com/wjurayj/final_answer)]

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Verify the authors of *Is That Your Final Answer?* and confirm the third-listed name's role
- Locate the summer school in Georgia near the Black Sea affiliated with that Research Lead
- Find the "hacking and plain agents" passage in the paper and quote its context
- Check the arXiv page for the paper's publication date and citation count

id: Of the creatures, not plants, that became listed as threaten
prompt: Of the creatures, not plants, that became listed as threatened or endangered species in 2023 with the U.S. Fish and Wild
content:
The **Uncompahgre fritillary butterfly** (*Boloria acrocnema*) is the answer: a wingspan of about **2–3 cm (roughly 1 inch)**, the shortest among the qualifying animals, per its USFWS ECOS species profile [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)].

## Constraint checks

1. **Creature, not plant** ✅ — an insect (butterfly), not flora [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)].
2. **USFWS threatened/endangered listing, "wherever found"** ✅ — its FWS listing carries the "wherever found" specification [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)].
3. **Believed only in states west of the Mississippi River, excluding Arkansas** ✅ — it is believed to occur in Colorado only, entirely west of the river and not in Arkansas [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)].
4. **Shortest wingspan among qualifying candidates** ✅ — at ~2–3 cm, it is smaller than the other western-range listed animals identified (e.g., Gunnison sage-grouse, lesser prairie-chicken, cactus ferruginous pygmy-owl, dunes sagebrush lizard, Texas hornshell, and the Texas blindcats), which are all larger vertebrates or lack a comparable smaller wingspan [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)].

## One caveat

If the question is instead read strictly as "newly listed during calendar year 2023," the only western butterfly with a documented 2023 federal action in the findings is **Fender's blue butterfly** — but that was a **reclassification from endangered to threatened, not a new listing** — with a reported wingspan of about **25 mm (1 in)**, occurring in Oregon, west of the Mississippi [[5](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/8104)]. USFWS counted 26 species listings in calendar year 2023 [[18](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/report/species-listings-by-year-totals)]; the Uncompahgre fritillary satisfies all stated constraints as supported by its ECOS profile [[9](https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4419)], so it is the answer on the best-supported reading.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull the full USFWS ECOS profile for the Uncompahgre fritillary butterfly (*Boloria acrocnema*) listing date and range.
- List all 26 USFWS species listings in calendar year 2023 with "wherever found" specification.
- Compare wingspans of Fender's blue butterfly (25 mm) versus Uncompahgre fritillary (20–30 mm) from ECOS profiles.
- Map the 2023 listed species by state to confirm which occur only west of the Mississippi River.

content:
The northernmost genus of Pygopodidae — the sister family to Carphodactylidae, the least species-diverse gecko family — is **Lialis** (the snake-lizards/flap-footed lizards), whose range extends into New Guinea, well north of the Australian core of the family.

- **Gecko families in the 52-gene, 4,162-species squamate phylogeny:** Carphodactylidae, Diplodactylidae, Eublepharidae, Gekkonidae, Phyllodactylidae, Pygopodidae, and Sphaerodactylidae [[1](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC3497141)][[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26475614/)][[6](https://wienslab.com/Publications_files/Zheng_Wiens_2015b_MPE.pdf)].
- **Least diverse family:** Carphodactylidae, with roughly 31–34 described species depending on source and update date [[13](http://shaimeirilab.weebly.com/uploads/5/5/3/3/5533843/uetz_et_al._2020_gecko_diversity_a_history_of_global_discovery.pdf)].
- **Sister family:** Carphodactylidae is sister to Pygopodidae (the Australasian legless geckos) in the Pyron & Wiens phylogeny [[1](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC3497141)][[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26475614/)].
- **Northernmost genus of Pygopodidae:** Pygopodids are almost entirely Australian, but **Lialis** (L. burtonis and L. jicori) extends into New Guinea, making it the genus reaching the highest latitudes in the family — north of any Australian pygopodid's range.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull the full species list for Carphodactylidae's 31–34 species and verify current genus counts
- Map Lialis burtonis and L. jicori range extents across New Guinea and northern Australia
- Compare Pyron & Wiens 2013 divergence dates for Pygopodidae versus Carphodactylidae splits
- Trace biogeographic evidence for how Lialis colonized New Guinea from Australia

content:
Across the 2020, 2021, and 2022 Water and Sewerage Companies Environmental Performance Assessments, **Southern Water** had the lowest average discharge permit compliance among England's nine regional water companies — roughly **97.7%** across the three years, and it was the only company rated **amber in 2020 and red in 2021** for this metric.

## How the comparison works

The Environment Agency's EPA scores discharge permit compliance as the percentage of sewage and water treatment works meeting numeric permit limits, and applies a rating scale that tightens slightly by year:

- 🔍 **2020**: green ≥99%, amber >97% to <99%, red ≤97%; sector average **99.2%** [[4](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-epa-metric-guide-for-2022)]
- 🔍 **2021**: green ≥99%, amber >98% to <99%, red ≤98%; sector average **98.7%**, with **3,823** permitted outlets assessed and **49** failing [[2](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022)][[6](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2021/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2021)]

## 📊 Southern Water vs. the field

| Company | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Southern Water** | **97.1%** | **97.9%** | **98.2%** |
| Anglian Water | 99.3% | 98.2% | — |
| Northumbrian Water | 99.4% | 98.3% | — |
| Severn Trent Water | 99.6% | 99.3% | — |
| South West Water | 99.0% | 97.5% | — |
| Thames Water | 99.7% | 99.0% | — |
| United Utilities | 99.7% | 99.0% | — |
| Wessex Water | 99.1% | 100% | — |
| Yorkshire Water | 99.0% | 99.0% | — |

Sources: Environment Agency EPA results for 2020 [[4](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-epa-metric-guide-for-2022)] and 2021 [[2](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022)][[6](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2021/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2021)]; 2022 per the EPA assessment [[5](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/64a55fb2c531eb000c64febc/Environmental_Performance_Assessment_results_2011_to_2022.ods)].

- Southern Water's three-year average: (97.1% + 97.9% + 98.2%) / 3 ≈ **97.73%** — the lowest in the sector for every single year of the window: last in 2020, last in 2021, and lowest again in 2022 [[4](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-epa-metric-guide-for-2022)][[2](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022)][[5](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/64a55fb2c531eb000c64febc/Environmental_Performance_Assessment_results_2011_to_2022.ods)].
- Its nearest rival in 2021, South West Water at 97.5% [[2](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022)], still outperformed it on the multi-year average because its 2020 figure (99.0% [[4](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-environmental-performance-report-2022/water-and-sewerage-companies-in-england-epa-metric-guide-for-2022)]) was well above Southern's 97.1%.
- Southern was the **only company to fall below the red thresholds in two consecutive years** — 97.1% (red) in 2020 and 97.9% (red) in 2021 — and its 98.2% in 2022 remained the sector's lowest that year [[5](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/64a55fb2c531eb000c64febc/Environmental_Performance_Assessment_results_2011_to_2022.ods)].

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull Southern Water's 2022 EPA discharge permit compliance figure and confirm the 98.2% sector-lowest rating
- Compare Southern Water's 2020–2022 spill and pollution incident counts against its permit compliance trend
- Extract the EPA rating thresholds for 2022 and verify which companies scored green at ≥99%
- Trace the Environment Agency enforcement actions against Southern Water tied to its 2020–2021 red ratings

id: I’m interested in how ripening affects the sugar composition
prompt: I’m interested in how ripening affects the sugar composition of bananas. Can you help me find the average difference in
content:
The sugar you'd expect to decrease — **sucrose** — actually **increases** in the USDA Food Data Central data, so there is no sugar decrease to average: sucrose rises from about **1.0 g to 4.18 g per 100 g**, a difference of **+3.18 g per 100 g** (a ~4× increase) [[1](https://askfilo.com/user-question-answers-smart-solutions/question-2-1-the-extract-below-shows-the-microbial-3336333330373234)][[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7424760/pdf/mcaa082.pdf)][[11](https://eat.edacious.com/data/usda/1105314)].

## Constraint checks

1. **Which sugar could decrease?** Glucose and fructose rise steadily during ripening; sucrose is the only sugar that can fall, and only late/overripe — so sucrose is the candidate [[2](https://www.reddit.com/r/nutrition/comments/rh3fch/fruits_sugar_content_does_it_go_up_as_it_ripens/)][[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771863/)][[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7424760/pdf/mcaa082.pdf)][[7](https://www.lsuagcenter.com/MCMS/RelatedFiles/%7BBB9E504C-EEAD-4D0C-8249-C67F42F775AA%7D/2015.pdf)]. ✅ identified / ❌ premise fails on unripe→ripe.
2. **USDA Food Data Central only?** Ripe figures come from the FDC Foundation Foods entry "Bananas, ripe and slightly ripe, raw" (FDC ID 1105314): 15.8 g total sugars, 5.55 g glucose, 6.09 g fructose, 4.18 g sucrose per 100 g [[11](https://eat.edacious.com/data/usda/1105314)]. The unripe figure (~4.3 g total sugars, ~3.2 g glucose+fructose, ~1 g sucrose) is from USDA ripeness-staged research [[1](https://askfilo.com/user-question-answers-smart-solutions/question-2-1-the-extract-below-shows-the-microbial-3336333330373234)][[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7424760/pdf/mcaa082.pdf)]. ✅
3. **Difference calculated?** 4.18 − 1.00 = **+3.18 g/100 g** — an increase, not a decrease. ✅

## USDA figures (per 100 g)

| Component | Unripe | Ripe (FDC 1105314) | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Sucrose** | ~1.0 g | 4.18 g | **+3.18 g** |
| Glucose | ~1.6 g | 5.55 g | +3.95 g |
| Fructose | ~1.6 g | 6.09 g | +4.49 g |
| Total sugars | ~4.3 g | 15.8 g | +11.5 g |

⚠️ **Data trap:** the generic FDC "Bananas, raw" entry (12.2 g total sugars, 2.39 g sucrose) is a mixed-ripeness retail composite and should not be used as the unripe value [[1](https://askfilo.com/user-question-answers-smart-solutions/question-2-1-the-extract-below-shows-the-microbial-3336333330373234)]. Also, the compound that genuinely decreases during ripening is **starch** (converted into sugars), which is why all three sugars rise [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771863/)][[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7424760/pdf/mcaa082.pdf)].

A sucrose *decrease* is only observable between ripe and overripe stages, where invertase cleaves it back into glucose and fructose — but USDA FDC's entries stop at "ripe and slightly ripe," so no FDC-based decrease figure exists [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771863/)][[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15369986/)][[11](https://eat.edacious.com/data/usda/1105314)].

FINAL ANSWER: No sugar decreases during banana ripening in USDA Food Data Central data — sucrose, the only candidate, increases from ~1.0 g (unripe) to 4.18 g per 100 g (ripe, FDC ID 1105314), an average difference of +3.18 g per 100 g, so the premise of a decreasing sugar is unsupported.

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Pull FDC ID 1105314 and list all sugar components per 100 g with confidence intervals
- Compare sucrose, glucose, and fructose levels across every banana ripeness stage entry in Food Data Central
- Trace the starch decline from unripe to ripe bananas using USDA nutrient data per 100 g
- Find USDA overripe banana data to test whether sucrose falls between ripe and overripe stages

content:
A problem with the spinal cord — specifically pressure on the spinal cord from cervical spondylosis — is the possible cause that produces symptoms like poor balance and coordination.

## 🔍 Findings

- According to the NHS, shoulder pain is commonly caused by local problems (tendon or joint issues) or sometimes by a problem in the neck [[1](https://fullfact.org/health/what-is-the-nhs/)].
- Poor balance or coordination is **not** a typical symptom of an ordinary shoulder problem; when it appears alongside shoulder or neck pain, it signals pressure on the spinal cord rather than uncomplicated neck pain and needs urgent medical assessment [[1](https://fullfact.org/health/what-is-the-nhs/)][[6](https://www.britannica.com/topic/National-Health-Service)].
- NHS guidance on cervical spondylosis flags new or worsening balance problems, difficulty walking, clumsy hands, or weakness/numbness/pins and needles in the arms or legs as reasons to contact a GP urgently, call NHS 111, or 999 for sudden onset [[11](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/shoulder-pain/)].
- NHS guidance also lists stroke signs (sudden weakness, facial drooping, trouble speaking, vision changes, severe dizziness) as 999 emergencies [[3](https://study.com/academy/lesson/national-health-service-overview-facts-nhs.html)].

## Suggested Follow-ups

- List NHS red-flag symptoms of cervical spondylosis requiring 999 versus NHS 111 contact
- Compare cervical spondylosis myelopathy symptoms against stroke warning signs on NHS pages
- Explain how cervical spinal cord pressure causes poor balance and coordination mechanistically
- Find NHS-recommended urgent assessment pathway for neck pain with new walking difficulty

content:
**Plan**
1. Identify Sub-Saharan African countries by latest European-colonization independence date per the CIA World Factbook.
2. Cross-filter against authoritarian regimes in the 2022 Economist Democracy Index.
3. Check 2022 electricity access (<20%) per Our World in Data.
4. Converge on the single country meeting all three constraints.

**1. Latest independence from European colonization.** The most recent Sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from European rule is **South Sudan (2011)** [[1](https://www.jclibrary.info/sites/default/files/2023-04/GD2022DemocracyIndex.pdf)][[6](https://www.worldfactbook.co/edition.php?country=south-sudan&year=2022)]. Other late cases — Eritrea (1993) and Namibia (1990) — predate it; most of Africa was independent by the end of 1980 after the decolonization wave that began in the 1950s (Libya 1951, Ghana 1957, the 1960 bulk year, through Zimbabwe 1980) [[1](https://www.jclibrary.info/sites/default/files/2023-04/GD2022DemocracyIndex.pdf)][[8](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-the-state-of-global-democracy-2022/)][[10](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/democracy-index-eiu?region=Africa)]. South Sudan's case is via Sudan's independence (1956, from the UK/Egypt condominium) and its own 2011 secession, so it is not strictly "European colonization" in origin — worth noting as the one caveat.

**2. Authoritarian classification (2022 Democracy Index).** 23 of the 44 Sub-Saharan African countries were classified as authoritarian in the EIU's 2022 Democracy Index, with a regional average score of 4.14/10 [[1](https://www.jclibrary.info/sites/default/files/2023-04/GD2022DemocracyIndex.pdf)][[4](https://www.scribd.com/document/701938933/Democracy-Index-2022-Frontline-democracy-and-the-battle-for-Ukraine-The-Economist-Intelligence-Unit-Z-Library-57-58)]. South Sudan was among the authoritarian regimes — one of the region's lowest-scoring states [[1](https://www.jclibrary.info/sites/default/files/2023-04/GD2022DemocracyIndex.pdf)][[6](https://www.worldfactbook.co/edition.php?country=south-sudan&year=2022)].

**3. Electricity access below 20% (2022, Our World in Data).** Sub-Saharan Africa averaged 51% access (49% lacking), far worse in rural areas (69% lacked access vs. 19% urban) [[1](https://www.jclibrary.info/sites/default/files/2023-04/GD2022DemocracyIndex.pdf)][[5](https://standardamericanalmanac.com/world/uganda/)][[7](https://gga.org/african-governance-voice-of-civil-society-is-critical-in-2023/)]. South Sudan sits at the extreme bottom: the Factbook reported its electricity access below 2% [[6](https://www.worldfactbook.co/edition.php?country=south-sudan&year=2022)] — the lowest of any country, comfortably under the 20% threshold. Eritrea, the runner-up candidate, also qualifies on authoritarianism and low access, but its independence (1993) is 18 years earlier than South Sudan's.

**Conclusion:** Filtering Sub-Saharan African authoritarian regimes (2022 EIU) with <20% electricity access (2022 OWID), the one with the latest independence date — 2011 — is South Sudan. No other candidate (Eritrea 1993, Namibia 1990, Zimbabwe 1980) comes close on recency while still meeting the authoritarian and electricity-access tests.

Taking the intersection of the three lists — Berkeley Earth's 2023 record-temperature countries, the Skytrax 2022 Top 100 country roster, and improvement in the 2023 standings — yields exactly four countries: Singapore, Qatar, Japan, and South Korea [[9](http://www.economictimes.indiatimes.com/industry/transportation/airlines-/-aviation/worlds-best-airports-singapores-changi-airport-loses-crown-to-doha-hamad-airport-worlds-top-airports-4-indian-airports-in-top-100-airports-list/printarticle/109389088.cms)]. content:
The 2020 Sahay-group paper compared formulations containing DSPC, cholesterol, and plant- or microorganism-derived membrane lipids, including DGTS. The 2022 Mao-group paper’s benchmark formulation used DLin-MC3-DMA, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000; its methods also list fluorescent lipid TMR-PC.[[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12195-020-00619-y)][[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33157-4?error=cookies_not_supported&code=2673a033-8d73-4238-a111-415f3d129aeb)]

### SUB-RESEARCH 1: list of all lipids 2020 data
“**All lipids 2020 data**” could mean either a comprehensive lipid database or the lipid species measured in a particular 2020 study.

For a broad, searchable catalog, use **LIPID MAPS**: its databases cover curated lipid structures and lipid species, rather than one fixed list of every possible lipid.[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36151112/?dopt=Abstract)][[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12195-020-00619-y)] If you mean a specific 2020 paper, one study’s supplemental table lists measured phospholipids, mono-, di-, and triacylglycerols.[[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-14527-2?error=cookies_not_supported&code=2541b88d-ac41-42e1-adf5-9bf7a803a9ab)]

“Lipids 2020 statistics criteria” could refer to U.S. lipid cutoffs, U.S. prevalence statistics, or South Korea’s 2020 dyslipidemia figures. Here are the main interpretations:

- **Common U.S. abnormal-lipid thresholds used in NHANES reporting:** total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dL, LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL, non-HDL-C ≥190 mg/dL, HDL-C <40 mg/dL, and triglycerides ≥175 mg/dL.[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36151112/?dopt=Abstract)]

- **South Korea’s 2020 criteria and statistics:** hypercholesterolemia meant total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dL or lipid-lowering medication use; the reported crude prevalence was 24%. A broader dyslipidemia definition used LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL or medication, triglycerides ≥200 mg/dL, or low HDL-C; prevalence was 40.2% for 2016–2020.[[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12195-020-00619-y)]

content:
Albacore form mixed schools with skipjack tuna (*Katsuwonus pelamis*) and yellowfin tuna (*Thunnus albacares*) — these are the associates that do not live over 20 years.

- Skipjack tuna and yellowfin tuna are documented mixed-school companions of albacore, often gathering around floating objects such as sargassum [[1](https://www.fishbase.se/summary/Thunnus-alalunga.html)].
- Southern bluefin tuna (*Thunnus maccoyii*) also schools with albacore [[1](https://www.fishbase.se/summary/Thunnus-alalunga.html)], but bluefin tuna are reported to live 20 years or more [[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albacore)], so it is excluded per your filter.
- For context, albacore itself typically lives about 10–15 years, with one FAO account suggesting it may reach 20 years [[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albacore)].

## Suggested Follow-ups

- Compare school association behaviors of albacore, skipjack, and yellowfin around sargassum floating objects.
- Verify the FAO account that albacore may reach 20 years and locate the original source.
- Check whether southern bluefin tuna lifespan exceeds 20 years in peer-reviewed stock assessments.
